title: Bowman weighs broader inflation against tighter financing for housing and AI
summary: Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman backed the October hold at 3.75–4.00 percent to allow time for the September increase and tighter financial conditions to work through the economy. By November 10 she was giving inflation more weight as the labour market had stabilised. She incorporated the October CPI release into an estimate that twelve-month core PCE inflation had probably risen to 3.3 percent. That was a forecast of a different price index, with the official October PCE report still to come. She named no preferred December rate change.

Bowman saw robust spending and investment alongside a less buoyant picture for households relying on labour income. She cited 2.4 percent first-half GDP growth and estimated third-quarter growth above 3 percent. A footnote warns that first-half growth might have been overstated by about 0.3 percentage point because revised retail sales had yet to be incorporated. Unemployment was 4.1 percent in October and payroll gains averaged about 80,000 per month through then. Both hiring and layoffs were subdued. Twelve-month wage growth was 3.1 percent in the September employment cost index wage component and the October average hourly earnings measure. Given productivity gains, she saw little evidence that labour costs were the source of above-target inflation.

For the twelve months through September, Bowman attributed approximately one quarter each of the core PCE overshoot to tariffs, energy and AI-related pressure. She associated the remaining quarter with earlier inflation shocks. The denominator is inflation above target, not all inflation. She expected tariff effects to fade and, eventually, greater supply and productivity to damp prices. The risk was that strong demand for scarce chips and equipment, freight costs or energy pass-through would keep broadening before those mechanisms took hold. A sector-specific origin does not rule out economy-wide implications through expectations or input costs.

Her financial analysis presents an opposing force on demand. Higher mortgage rates had weighed on housing, corporate spreads had widened and the dollar had strengthened. AI investment was increasingly drawing on external finance. She said related debt was on course to exceed $800 billion this year and estimated potential payments on leases, contracts and residual-value guarantees at over three times the debt amount. These are different exposure measures. Guarantees can redistribute the same project risk, and potential future obligations are not outstanding debt due immediately. Large technology companies supplied guarantees that smaller developers could pledge, and some hardware suppliers invested in businesses buying their products. Bowman described apparent circular financing, while acknowledging that most of the exposed institutions had stable funding and adequate capital. Banks, insurers, pension funds, private credit and mutual funds had exposure. Interconnected claims made the final counterparty risk difficult to assess. Bowman viewed wider bond spreads and higher credit default swap costs for some AI companies as possible signs that investors were reassessing returns; she gave no implied default probability or recovery estimate. Higher funding costs could delay projects even if long-run AI adoption remained strong.

Before the conflict roughly one fifth of global oil supply passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Brent had exceeded $110 a barrel in the second half of October and then fallen sharply. Gulf crude flows had nearly recovered, but freight and insurance remained expensive. Refinery damage had widened margins for finished fuels before part of the increase reversed. The futures curve implied a gradual decline, with global consumption expected to exceed supply through at least year-end. Bowman put the US strategic reserve at just under 50 days of crude imports. New Gulf pipeline capacity was due in early 2027 and later, offering limited help with immediate delivery costs. Renewed disruption would put the greatest pressure on lower- and middle-income households’ purchasing power.

Bowman saw a reason to guard against persistent inflation and a reason to weigh carefully what another hike would do to interest-sensitive sectors. Her conditional baseline was stable employment and core inflation moving closer to 2 percent next year as special factors waned. A renewed energy disruption could instead raise prices while reducing households’ purchasing power. Disappointing AI revenue could produce a different outcome, with lower investment and weaker price pressure together. The October loan officer survey already showed weak demand concentrated in real estate lending. October PCE and November employment data were still ahead. The first delivery was scheduled for 3:30 p.m. EST, after the CPI data she used; the Fed says she repeated the same remarks later that day.

questions.question: Does Bowman’s inflation decomposition survive changes in category assignment?
questions.detail: Map tariff exposure, energy inputs and data-centre demand to price categories and account for overlaps. Calculate contributions to the excess over 2 percent. Use subsequent official PCE data to evaluate the October estimate separately from the September attribution. BEA component weights and published input-price and import data would help separate overlapping exposures from measured inflation.

questions.question: Which AI financing obligations create independent losses?
questions.detail: Trace one project from end-customer revenue through its lease, residual-value guarantee and secured equipment debt to each ultimate holder. Use issuer filings, financing agreements and debt maturities to estimate when a cash shortfall would occur, who must fund it first and who bears losses after collateral is sold. This would distinguish separate exposures from multiple claims on the same revenue stream.

questions.question: Would an energy shock become a broader inflation problem or a demand drag?
questions.detail: Track freight, insurance and refining margins alongside crude prices, consumer expectations and discretionary spending by income group. The sequence and breadth of these changes would help distinguish second-round pricing from a loss of real household purchasing power. Check delivered fuel prices and household spending surveys alongside the futures curve Bowman describes.

questions.question: How much restraint was already passing through financial markets?
questions.detail: Compare mortgage rates, lending standards, spreads and investment plans across housing, small firms and large technology borrowers. Distinguish the speech’s afternoon information set from earlier same-day CPI and Fed communication before studying Treasury or equity prices. Use the October loan officer survey and issuer-level borrowing terms to distinguish declining credit demand from a restriction in supply. Treat the later repeat delivery as a separate time stamp.
